Arabidopsis Atlas · Metabolome story

How much does Arabidopsis metabolism vary between accessions, and does it repeat?

Three published natural-variation metabolome panels (leaves before and after six days of darkness, leaves under control and stress, and primary metabolism in whole rosettes) share one accession key. Put side by side, they show which differences between accessions repeat from one experiment to the next, how darkness and stress compare, and where the atlas ecotypes sit. The public MetaboLights Arabidopsis studies show what else has been measured.

02Does a metabolite rank accessions the same way twice?

If an accession is high for a metabolite in one experiment, is it high in another?

Zhu's and Wu's 2018 leaf experiments agree well. Across about $lc_acc shared accessions, $lc_sig of the $lc_n metabolites matched between them rank accessions alike (BH q < 0.05), with a median Spearman ρ of $lc_rho. Glucosinolates and flavonols repeat best; the top is $lc_best (ρ $lc_best_rho).

The GC-MS and LC-MS panels agree far less. Wu 2016 and Wu 2018 share $gc_n named compounds across $gc_acc accessions, and their median ρ is $gc_rho. Only $gc_sig agree significantly, led by proline (ρ $proline_rho) and citric acid (ρ $citric_rho). This is not a measure of platform error. The two experiments also differ in what was harvested (whole rosettes vs leaves) and in how plants were grown; Wu 2018's growth stage has not been checked here.

03Darkness and stress move metabolites alike

Zhu's six days of darkness against Wu's stress treatment, for the metabolites both measured.

For each metabolite, the median per-accession change under darkness (Zhu, 6 d minus 0 d) is set against the median change under Wu's stress treatment (stress minus control). $agree of the $agree_n metabolites move in the same direction (two-sided binomial p = $agree_p). The branched-chain amino acids leucine and isoleucine rise most in both. Wu's supplement describes its stress as 32 °C darkness; that has not yet been checked against the paper's methods.

04Primary metabolites co-vary a little within their class

Wu 2016's GC-MS panel: $gc_named named metabolites across $gc_cor_acc accessions.

Across accessions, two amino acids, two organic acids or two sugars correlate slightly more than metabolites from different classes: the median ρ is $within within a class and $between between classes. The strongest pairs are close relatives. Some pairs share a quantification ion (m/z 160 for altrose, glucose and mannose; m/z 158 for leucine and isoleucine), so part of their correlation may be one derivatised signal. Read the pairs as co-variation, not shared regulation.

05Where the atlas ecotypes sit

The six ecotypes shaped in the 3D atlas, placed within each panel's range of accessions.

Col-0 (the ecotype flown in NASA's OSD-522 experiment) sits between the ${col0_min}th and ${col0_max}th percentile in every class shown. It is lowest for amino acids in Wu 2018's control leaves (percentile $col0_aa_lc) and also below the middle for amino acids in the GC-MS rosettes ($col0_aa_gc). It is highest for flavonoids ($col0_flav). The other five atlas ecotypes spread much more widely, from percentile $others_min to $others_max.

Methods and limits

Values stay on each study's published scale (Zhu: BLUPs; Wu 2018: log2-scale intensity; Wu 2016: normalised intensity), so panels are compared by ranks and directions, never by absolute level. Correlations are Spearman over the accessions both experiments share (at least 20), with Benjamini–Hochberg correction within each comparison. Wu 2018 reports some metabolites in both ion modes, which sit on different levels, so each metabolite uses one ion mode throughout (scripts/wu_modes.py). Metabolites are matched across panels only by Zhu–Wu formula and retention-time pairs or by identical names; synonyms such as malate and malic acid stay apart, so some real matches are missed. Wu et al. 2018 is not open access; its per-accession values are shown with citation for research use.
